item.title: [The Boston Globe] Chad Tracy hopes to have Willson Contreras back by the start of the playoffs - The Boston Globe
item.dc:creator: Tim Healey

item.content:encoded:
Willson Contreras remained absent from the Red Sox’ lineup Thursday night at Fenway Park, seven days after he got hit by a pitch and bruised his right hand.
Is it fair to say he will be ready for the start of the playoffs?
“I hope so,” manager Chad Tracy said before the team’s finale with the Guardians. “I hope so. But [the Red Sox] want to see how he gets through all this stuff and where he’s at. And my hope is — at least for now — that he swings and feels even better than he did the other day, and then we’ll go from there.”
The first baseman took batting practice in the indoor cage, as he did earlier in the week.
It would be “huge,” Tracy said, if he was ready in time to play at any point during the Cubs series. Otherwise, he may well roll into the AL Wild Card Series without having faced live pitching in nearly two weeks.
“But I also think you’re talking about a guy [who has] a pretty good idea of his swing,” Tracy said. “[With] Willson not being down that long, the most important thing is that he’s healthy. So if he’s healthy and feeling good about it, where we’re able to get him some at-bats, that’d be great. But we’re still going to be reactive to how he’s feeling.”
Weather watch
The Cubs-Red Sox series remains in flux.
They will attempt to play a doubleheader at Fenway Park on Friday, with 1 p.m. and 6 p.m. first pitches, before a potential nor’easter arrives.
Yet to be decided: where and when the teams play their regular-season finale. Although it is scheduled for 7:15 p.m. Saturday in Boston, it could be moved to another venue, such as Tampa Bay, if the weekend forecast remains horrendous.
If the game is moved, the clubs would leave Friday night and likely play at 3 p.m. Sunday, same as all of the other finales.
MLB and the teams intend to make a call by midday Friday about what to do about Game 162.
“In a nutshell, it doesn’t look good. That’s basically what I’ve heard,” Tracy said of the weather. “Seems like we should be able to get that [doubleheader] in even [if during] the second game there might be a little bit of drizzle or whatever. It doesn’t look bad, at least what I’m seeing, and then figure out what happens next.”
Crochet on the move
A wrinkle from the weather: Garrett Crochet (left shoulder injury) will head to Fort Myers, Fla., on Friday so that he can throw an inning of live batting practice on Saturday.
The Sox have a stash of Triple-A hitters, including infielders Romy Gonzalez and Franklin Arias, working out at Fenway South.
Rafaela OK
Ceddanne Rafaela turned out to be just fine after a scare Wednesday.
The Thursday MRI on his right hamstring came back “clean,” Tracy said, affirming Rafaela’s stance from the night prior that his exit after two innings was no big deal.
“The feel is that it was a cramp, probably actually precipitated by the diving catch an inning prior],” Tracy said. “He tends to dive, and he does have low back/hip stuff that throws him out of the line for a second, that’ll manifest itself in feeling [the hamstring].”
Rafaela was back in the lineup against the Guardians, batting sixth and playing center field. It was his second game back from a right quad strain.
Major honors from minors
The Red Sox announced their annual minor league award winners, a group headed by Arias, the offensive player of the year. He slashed .323/.400/.557 with 25 homers and 91 RBIs in 117 games with Double-A Portland and Triple-A Worcester, emerging as one of the top prospects in all of the minors.
Lefthander Dylan Brown was named pitcher of the year. A 22-year-old starter, he had a 3.46 ERA and 143 strikeouts in 106⅔ innings with Low-A Salem and High-A Greenville.
Other honored were catcher Gerardo Rodriguez (defensive player of the year), outfielder Andrews Opata (baserunner of the year), outfielder Joskairo Ramirez (Latin program position player of the year), and righthander Emanuel Jimenez (Latin program pitcher of the year).
Mead update
Infielder Curtis Mead (left wrist fracture) plans to take another step forward Friday by taking batting practice off of a machine. He will head to Fort Myers with Crochet and potentially hit against him on Saturday, he said. He is not ruled out for the first round of the playoffs beginning Tuesday, but that deadline might be too soon … Tracy left Roman Anthony out of the lineup to give him a day off. The outfielder had started 22 consecutive games since returning from the IL, batting .242 with a .726 OPS … Eli White was back at Fenway for the first time since season-ending right foot surgery Tuesday. He said he is due for a three-month recovery. That timeline would allow the outfielder to get almost all the way back to full health before the expected lockout on Dec. 1, at which point teams will not be allowed to communicate with players … Infielder Anthony Seigler said he was diagnosed with a carpal boss, a bony lump on the back of his right hand/wrist — the same injury that plagued catcher Connor Wong last year. Wong wound up having surgery to get it removed. Seigler said he has not discussed that possibility with the Red Sox … DH/outfielder Masataka Yoshida (left hamstring strain) appeared on the field at Fenway, playing catch and doing light agility drills … Dustin Pedroia and his family, in town this week, were on the field about five hours before first pitch against Cleveland, chatting with Red Sox personnel. His three sons made sure to poke their head into the Green Monster.

item.content:encoded:
Ceddanne Rafaela is back in the Red Sox lineup a day after leaving Wednesday night’s game with a right hamstring tightness.
The Red Sox outfielder will bat sixth and start in center field for Thursday night’s finale against the Cleveland Guardians.
“He’s good,” Red Sox manager Chad Tracy said pregame Thursday. “All the scans last night were clean, we did an MRI as a precaution, all clean, subjectively he feels really good, so seems exactly what it was, the feel is it was a cramp.”
Rafaela left Wednesday’s game in the top of the third inning after initially feeling tightness during his first at bat in the bottom of the second. He had just been activated from the injured list earlier that day after missing 17 games with a right quad strain, though Rafaela expressed optimism postgame that the hamstring issue was far less serious.
Losing Rafaela again so soon before the playoffs would have been a huge blow to the Red Sox. The outfielder is a favorite to win his second Gold Glove in center field and has enjoyed a strong season at the plate, batting .284 with 16 home runs, 17 stolen bases and a .763 OPS.
Though Rafaela won’t miss any more time, Willson Contreras remains out of the lineup with a bruised hand after being hit by a pitch last Thursday in Texas. Contreras has now been sidelined for a week, and the plan was for him to run through a battery of hitting drills in the cages and on the field Thursday to see how his hand is progressing.
While the hope is he will be ready to return soon, Tracy acknowledged that isn’t a guarantee.
“I hope so, but I want to see how he gets through all this stuff and where he’s at, and my hope is at least for now that he feels even better than he did the other day and we’ll go from there.”
Tracy added that while it would be great for Contreras to get some at bats before the regular season ends, he hasn’t missed much time and has a good idea of his swing, so it wouldn’t be an issue if he didn’t play before the postseason.
“The most important thing is he’s healthy,” Tracy said. “So if he’s healthy and feeling good about it where we can get him some at bats, that’d be great, but we’re still going to be reactive to how he’s feeling.”
Minor League awards
Top prospect Franklin Arias highlighted the Red Sox minor league award winners, earning Offensive Player of the Year recognition. The 20-year-old shortstop enjoyed a dominant season in which he batted .323 with 25 home runs, 91 RBI and a .957 OPS over 117 games across Double-A and Triple-A, and he finishes the year ranked as MLB’s No. 2 prospect according to Baseball America.
The other recipients include left-hander Dylan Brown (Pitcher of the Year), catcher Gerardo Rodriguez (Defensive Player of the Year), outfielder Andrews Opata (Baserunner of the Year), outfielder Joskairo Ramirez (Latin Program Position Player of the Year) and right-hander Emanuel Jimenez (Latin Program Pitcher of the Year).
Right-hander Wyatt Olds is also being recognized as the 2026 recipient of the Lou Gorman Award, which annually honors a Red Sox minor leaguer who demonstrates perseverance to make his big league debut.
Extra innings
With heavy rain expected throughout the weekend the Red Sox plan to send left-hander Garrett Crochet to Fort Myers on Friday so he can throw his next live batting practice session on Saturday. The expectation is he will throw one inning but probably more pitches than the 16 he threw on Tuesday. Depending on how things go the club will decide whether or not to add him to the Wild Card roster. … Roman Anthony, who is also not in Thursday’s lineup, is being given a day off his feet to rest, Tracy said. … Back in the clubhouse wearing a walking boot following his foot surgery earlier this week, outfielder Eli White confirmed he’ll be non-weight bearing for several weeks and will miss the remainder of the season. … Infielder Anthony Seigler (right wrist inflammation) has resumed taking ground balls and ran through a series of drills Thursday. … The Red Sox have not determined who will start Game 1 and 2 of next week’s AL Wild Card Series.

item.title: [bosoxinjection.com] Red Sox might've cemented Craig Breslow’s rise off the hot seat too soon
item.dc:creator: Brian Burrows

item.content:encoded:
The Craig Breslow era in Boston has felt like a roller coaster ride. Hired at the start of the 2023-24 offseason, the Boston Red Sox have not had a losing season under Breslow, despite wild swings in the team's form over the three years.
With the Red Sox clinching a playoff berth for the second year in a row, team ownership decided that now was the time to exercise two options on their Chief Baseball Officer's contract, guaranteeing his deal for the 2029 and 2030 seasons. On the surface, a head of baseball operations who got his team to the playoffs in years two and three of their time running the club getting years added to their contract, would make sense, but in Breslow's case it isn't as straightforward.
It was only three months ago when most of Red Sox Nation was calling for Breslow's head. The Red Sox were 32-46 on June 24, dead last in the division, and it already seemed like the season was over. It took a miraculous turnaround to get the team to the playoffs. Not to say that Breslow had nothing to do with that; he had added a lot of players to the roster who were key contributors, but that has a lot more to do with the players and coaches than the front office.
Breslow's tenure has also been marred by controversy, specifically the Rafael Devers drama. It was his handling of the situation, along with former manager Alex Cora, that ultimately led to the fracture of the relationship with the team's then-face of the franchise. While the fanbase was split on whose side they took, player or team, his actions after the fact didn't make it any better.
Red Sox's Craig Breslow had the hottest seat of any GM only three months ago
It was the signing of Alex Bregman that caused the Devers drama in the first place. While Breslow was praised for the signing, Bregman opted out at the end of the year and was then not re-signed. The Red Sox went from two elite third basemen to none in the span of a season. It wasn't a good look for the Red Sox CBO.
Now, Breslow's pivot from all of the drama and mess surrounding Devers and Bregman looks incredibly good in hindsight. The additions of Ranger Suarez, Sonny Gray, Willson Contreras, Caleb Durbin, and others have been extremely impactful to the Red Sox's success this season. While some of those moves were celebrated at the time they happened, others like the Durbin-Kyle Harrison swap (that also netted the Red Sox Andruw Monasterio and Anthony Seigler) were heavily scrutinized.
Breslow also made good moves at the trade deadline, adding Erik Miller and Eli White, who have looked good for the Sox. He also made the splash trade for Adley Rutschman, which hasn't worked as well on the field, but certainly instilled confidence in the team, knowing the front office believed in them.
Red Sox could've softened the impact by extending one of Craig Breslow's options at first
All of this is to say that Breslow's time as CBO hasn't been as smooth sailing as the records would suggest. He has had some high highs but also some low lows. Why did ownership feel the need to exercise both options right now? The first option wasn't needed until the 2029 season, two years out. The second was for 2030, three years out.
Doing the first one now would've been fine — picking up the 2029 option gives Breslow another three comfortable seasons on his contract. That would make him more comfortable making moves for the future and give him the job security to know he will likely be in place to see them play out. Selecting the 2030 option on the same day was unnecessary, though.
There have been too many hiccups in the three years under Breslow to say he has warranted another four seasons. The start of 2026 could easily repeat itself in 2027. Should ownership feel the need to relieve him of his duties early, then this makes it that much harder. Breslow hasn't won a World Series in Boston; in fact, he hasn't even made it out of the Wild Card round. Exercising the option for 2030 feels very premature.
Breslow has not done a bad job in Boston. At the end of the day, it's results that matter, and Breslow's teams have made the playoffs two out of three times. He shouldn't be fearing for his job, but his contract also wasn't ending for another two seasons. It feels early to be handing him the keys so far down the road after the drama of his first two years as CBO.

item.title: [bostonherald.com] Red Sox mailbag: Should Garrett Crochet, Tanner Houck be on playoff roster?
item.dc:creator: Mac Cerullo
item.description: Can you believe the playoffs are almost here? A week from today the Red Sox will wrap up their regular season, closing the book on what has been among the most unexpected, topsy turvy seasons we’ve ever seen. From there the playoffs await, and who knows what twists and turns may still be in store. But before we get there, what business is there left for the Red Sox to get squared away before Game 1 of the Wild Card series? We answer your questions in today’s Red Sox mailbag. Tanner Houck and Gar
item.content:encoded:
Can you believe the playoffs are almost here? A week from today the Red Sox will wrap up their regular season, closing the book on what has been among the most unexpected, topsy turvy seasons we’ve ever seen. From there the playoffs await, and who knows what twists and turns may still be in store.
But before we get there, what business is there left for the Red Sox to get squared away before Game 1 of the Wild Card series? We answer your questions in today’s Red Sox mailbag.
Tanner Houck and Garrett Crochet both appear close to ready to return. What is the chance that the Red Sox decide to put both of them on the postseason roster? Each feels like a high upside question mark but is it too risky relying on both of them to excel in limited roles? — Paul from Bluesky
If the Red Sox decide they’re ready I think there’s a great chance both pitch in the playoffs. The question of whether or not it’s too risky is valid, but the other factor to consider is would it be riskier to let an inferior arm take the mound at Yankee Stadium with the season on the line.
The nature of a best-of-three playoff series compared to a best-of-five or even a best-of-seven also makes the idea of loading up on short-inning relievers more attractive.
The Red Sox will only need three starting pitchers in the first round, presumably Sonny Gray, Ranger Suarez and Payton Tolle, in some order. That effectively frees up two additional bullpen spots, one of which I’m guessing will be filled by Jake Bennett as an emergency bulk man should the starter exit early due to injury or poor performance.
The back end of the bullpen is pretty much set in stone. If everyone is healthy and available it will be Aroldis Chapman, Garrett Whitlock, Erik Miller and Tyron Guerrero locking down the high leverage innings. But after that the Red Sox have some interesting decisions to make.
In one group you have the other short men, including Greg Weissert, Jovani Moran and Wyatt Olds. Then in the next group you have the longer men, including Patrick Sandoval, Brayan Bello, Alec Gamboa and Raymond Burgos. Finally, you have Crochet, Houck and Johan Oviedo, who has also begun a rehab assignment after missing nearly the entire season. What the Red Sox have to decide is which five of those 10 options give you the best chance to win?
I don’t think you can dispute that Crochet and Houck have the highest ceiling of that bunch, so if they’re good to go I don’t think the Red Sox will hesitate to give them the nod.
With Romy Gonzalez now hitting so well in Worcester, do you see him being put on the postseason roster as a lefty masher, and one of Isiah Kiner-Falefa, Andruw Monasterio or Jahmai Jones being left off? — @wcbosox on Bluesky
If the Red Sox believe Romy Gonzalez gives them the best chance to win in October, I feel like it would make sense for them to call him up and get him some looks at big league pitching over the last two weeks. You could make a great case that they should — he was batting .360 in 23 games since being optioned to Triple-A entering Friday — but if that doesn’t happen then that could be a sign the Red Sox don’t see him as part of the October plan.
Either way, the club has some tough decisions to make as far as constructing the bench goes.
Presuming that Ceddanne Rafaela returns from the IL without any issues and Willson Contreras isn’t sidelined by his hand injury, the Red Sox should enter the playoffs with a starting lineup featuring Adley Rutschman at catcher, Contreras, Nick Sogard, Trevor Story and Caleb Durbin across the infield, and an outfield of Rafaela, Wilyer Abreu, Roman Anthony and Jarren Duran, with one of Anthony or Duran presumably starting at designated hitter if a righty is on the mound.
That leaves four spots for Kiner-Falefa, Monasterio, Jones, Mickey Gasper, Connor Wong, Nate Eaton, Gonzalez and possibly Curtis Mead. For our purposes we can probably set aside Eaton, who will likely be optioned upon Rafaela’s activation, as well as Mead, who only just started swinging a light bat and won’t have the benefit of a rehab assignment prior to his return.
Let’s also set aside some of the more outside the box candidates like Braiden Ward, who has never appeared in a big league game but who may garner consideration as a late-inning pinch runner after stealing 60 bases at Triple-A.
One spot will go to a backup catcher, and while you could talk yourself into Gasper filling that role, Wong has the most familiarity with the pitching staff and the Red Sox would probably rather keep Gasper available as a pinch hitter without worrying about catching logistics.
How about the other three spots? Kiner-Falefa, Monasterio and Gonzalez are all versatile infield defenders who bat right-handed, so there’s some redundancy there. Jones also bats right-handed and could function as an emergency reserve outfielder in addition to his pinch hitter, and while Gasper is technically a switch hitter, his real value comes from the left side, where he’s crushed righties over the past month.
What’s going to happen? My guess is the bench will be Wong, Gasper, Jones and one of the three righty infielders. So to go back to your original question, could Gonzalez make the playoff roster over one of Kiner-Falefa, Monasterio or Jones? Yes, and in fact even if he doesn’t make the roster one of those guys could still wind up on the outside looking in.
If the playoffs started today who would be the starting second baseman? Also, what’s the long-term plan for that position? — Tom P.
If the playoffs started today I think Nick Sogard would be the clear choice to start at second base. He’s been an everyday player for the Red Sox since the end of July, and at a time where most of the offense has hit a skid Sogard has been a reliable contributor at the plate, batting .262 with five home runs and a .772 OPS entering the weekend since being called back up on July 29.
Long-term, the Red Sox have a couple of different candidates who could emerge in the coming years.
If he hadn’t broken his wrist in his team debut I think it’s safe to say Curtis Mead would have spent the past two months starting at second for the Red Sox. Prior to the trade he was in the midst of a breakout season with the Washington Nationals, and at only 25 years old there’s good reason to believe his best years are still ahead of him. Whether he returns in the playoffs or for the start of next season, Mead should have the best chance to claim second base for himself.
But outside of him, Sogard and perhaps Gonzalez or Anthony Seigler, there is one other wild card. That’s Franklin Arias.
The top Red Sox prospect is putting the finishing touches on a brilliant season, and if he continues to develop he should have a great chance of becoming a key building block, perhaps as soon as next year. With Story under contract for only one more season he will have an opportunity to slide right into the starting shortstop job entering 2028, but what if he proves he’s ready for primetime before that? In that case Arias might get an initial look at second, with Mead perhaps rotating between the designated hitter spot and occasionally giving Durbin and Contreras a breather at their corner infield positions.
Does MLB need to readjust its postseason schedule? The No. 2 or 3 team in the American League will be eliminated in a three-game series, meanwhile two teams that are barely .500 play each other in the first round. — Brandon C.
I like the idea that there should be a reward for winning your division. If you’re one of the top two division winners you get a first round bye, and if you’re the third division winner you at least get to host the best-of-three Wild Card series. I’m fine with that, even in a weird year like this where all of the American League’s best teams are in the same division and the other division leaders are mediocre at best.
But the problem is what happens afterwards. Like you said, the No. 2 and 3 teams in the AL are probably going to wind up being the Yankees and Red Sox, and whichever of those teams advances will have to play the No. 1 seeded Tampa Bay Rays. Meanwhile, all three teams on the other side of the bracket could potentially finish with worse records than anyone on the AL East side, and one of those clubs will be guaranteed a trip to the ALCS.
I think MLB could address this by reseeding after the Wild Card round. The top two division winners would still get home field advantage in their divisional series, but whichever team advancing out of the Wild Card round has the better record would be paired with the second division winner. So this year if the Red Sox beat the Yankees and let’s say the AL West champion wins their Wild Card series, the Red Sox would go on to play the AL Central champion instead of the Rays, while the AL West champion would get Tampa Bay even though they would have technically started the playoffs as the higher seed.
Most years it probably won’t make a huge difference, but reseeding ahead of the divisional round would strike a balance between preserving the incentives for winning your division while ensuring the bracket doesn’t become unbalanced.

item.content:encoded:
Boston Red Sox third baseman Caleb Durbin dislocated his left pinky in late June. He reinjured it early last month.
Before the Red Sox’s upcoming series against the Tampa Bay Rays at Tropicana Field, Durbin told the Boston Globe’s (subscription required) Alex Speier his pinky is still bothering him.
Boston Red Sox 3B Caleb Durbin Makes Statement on Injury Before Rays series
Durbin said his pinky doesn’t “quite straighten or bend all the way.”
The third baseman received X-Rays after he initially injured his pinky in June and after he reinjured it in August. Both times, the X-rays revealed there was no fracture.
“There really is kind of a joint understanding [with the team] that we’ll get it looked at at the end of the season if we have to, because [whatever the diagnosis is], it’s not going to impact my decision to play at all,” Durbin said.
Speier asked Durbin if he needs offseason surgery.
“I don’t know yet. We’ll find out,” he said. “I hope there’s something we can do about it. But we’ll get there when the time comes.”
Read More: Pinkie injury may be affecting Caleb Durbin, but it’s not keeping him out of Red Sox lineup
Despite his pinky injury, Durbin hasn’t been placed on the injured list at all this season.
Looking at Boston Red Sox 3B Caleb Durbin
On Feb. 9, the Red Sox acquired Durbin, shortstop Andruw Monasterio, second baseman Anthony Seigler and future considerations from the Milwaukee Brewers for second baseman David Hamilton and left-handers Kyle Harrison and Shane Drohan.
Durbin, 26, has hit .248/.333/.381 with 13 home runs and 64 RBI over 145 games with Boston this year.
Durbin made his MLB debut with the Brewers last season. He hit .256/.334/.387 with 11 home runs and 53 RBI during his rookie year.
The Red Sox will begin their series against the Rays at 7:10 p.m. EDT on Friday.

item.title: [BoSox Injection] Red Sox fans may have spoken too soon on winner of Caleb Durbin-Kyle Harrison trade
item.dc:creator: Brandon Glick

Tack on the fact that Shane Drohan has become a valuable starter in his own right this year while Andruw Monasterio has been worth negative fWAR, and you'v
item.content:encoded:
We won't spend too long belaboring how bad the Kyle Harrison-Caleb Durbin looked for the Boston Red Sox after a few months; the southpaw had emerged as a genuine National League Cy Young contender for the Milwaukee Brewers in the first half, while the third baseman was one of the league's worst qualified hitters through the beginning of June. Tack on the fact that Shane Drohan has become a valuable starter in his own right this year while Andruw Monasterio has been worth negative fWAR, and you've got a recipe for an all-time disaster of a trade.
And yet, after the tide began shifting over the summer, we can now definitively say the pendulum has swung back in the other direction. Durbin has been a star since June 1, posting an .812 OPS and a 129 wRC+. Meanwhile, Harrison is struggling so badly that he's now been moved out of the Brewers' rotation entirely.
It's far too early to suggest that the Red Sox have made up that early gap and are now the winners of the blockbuster trade, but it's clear that their decision to go all-in for Durbin wasn't a foolish one.
Red Sox just need to break even now to win Caleb Durbin trade in the future
In that same post-June-1 span, Harrison has pitched to an 6.10 ERA and 5.38 FIP, allowing a whopping 17 home runs over just 59 innings. A bout with forearm tightness near the All-Star break definitely has something to do with his second-half collapse, but he hasn't been pitching like an ace for quite a while. The fact that there's been conversations about him being left off the Brewers' postseason roster entirely should tell you all you need to know about the southpaw's recent struggles.
Durbin is trending in the exact opposite direction, as he's currently the seventh-most valuable third baseman in the league by fWAR (2.9) this season. A lot of that has to do with how excellent his baserunning and glove have been, but saying that someone is above average in every phase of the game isn't exactly a bad thing. He's a couple of steals and some favorable votes away from a 20 SB, Gold Glove campaign in his Red Sox debut. Not too shabby, eh?
It's also worth factoring in the other players Craig Breslow pried out of Milwaukee; neither Monasterio nor Anthony Seigler have been great in limited duty in Boston, but the former has produced some timely hits while playing all four infield positions while the latter has a 102 wRC+ in just under 175 plate appearances this year.
Then there's Owen Hull, whom the Red Sox selected with the compensatory draft pick the Brewers forked over in the trade. All he did after being drafted was mash in High-A, posting a .967 OPS in 24 games.
With Durbin under contract through 2031 and Hull sure to fly up the prospect rankings over the offseason, there's a good chance that the Sox can win this trade down the road, so long as they continue to break even for now.

item.title: [NBC Sports Boston] Five biggest issues plaguing Red Sox with postseason looming
item.dc:creator: Justin Leger
item.description: The Boston Red Sox are still sitting comfortably in the second Wild Card spot, but there are several issues they must resolve before they start thinking about playoff baseball. item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox are still sitting comfortably in the second Wild Card spot, but there are several issues they must resolve before they start thinking about playoff baseball.
Boston is a mediocre 11-11 over its last 22 games. While that's been good enough to sustain its playoff position, its play hasn't exactly inspired optimism for a deep postseason run.
Most of the Red Sox' problems can be linked to their underperforming lineup. Key hitters like Roman Anthony, Willson Contreras, Adley Rutschman and Wilyer Abreu have been concerningly inconsistent.
A deeper dive into the numbers suggests the struggling Sox will have their work cut out for them in their presumed Wild Card Series rematch at Yankee Stadium. Here are the club's five biggest areas of concern with 10 games remaining:
Roman Anthony is ice-cold
The Red Sox need Roman Anthony to be one of their best offensive players to have any chance of a deep postseason run. If the former No. 1 prospect continues to play the way he has for most of September, that will be problematic.
Anthony is hitting just .149 (7-for-47) with one home run and a .428 OPS over his last 11 games. He has struck out 18 times in 51 plate appearances.
The 22-year-old's struggles beg the question: should he still be the leadoff hitter in the postseason? Interim manager Chad Tracy will have no choice but to reevaluate Anthony's spot in the lineup if his woes continue. The problem with that is there aren't any exciting alternatives. The leadoff spot has been a glaring issue all season long, regardless of who has been thrust into the role.
Struggling against high velocity
The Red Sox offense has been inconsistent no matter who's on the mound, but it has mostly struggled against pitchers with high velo. Here's how some of Boston's regulars have fared this season against pitches greater than or equal to 97 mph:
- Wilyer Abreu: .170 BA, .623 OPS (237 pitches)
- Jarren Duran: .065 BA, .300 OPS (203 pitches)
- Willson Contreras: .170 BA, .512 OPS (166 pitches)
- Ceddanne Rafaela: .205 BA, .449 OPS (157 pitches)
- Roman Anthony: .091 BA, .440 OPS (58 pitches)
- Adley Rutschman: .077 BA, .451 OPS (57 pitches)
The Red Sox' top performer against high velocity (97 mph and above) has been Caleb Durbin (.364 BA, .912 OPS, 161 pitches).
Being so vulnerable against high velocity will especially be a problem for Boston in its expected Wild Card Series matchup against the New York Yankees. Cy Young frontrunner and likely Game 1 starter Cam Schlittler averages 98 mph with his four-seam fastball, which he uses 44.5 percent of the time. Gerrit Cole averages 96.9 mph with his four-seam, using it 49.3 percent of the time.
Leaving runners stranded
Boston has been below average all season at capitalizing on runners in scoring position. It currently ranks 17th in batting average (.250) and 21st in OPS (.731) with RISP. They're hitting just .212 in such situations through 14 games so far in September.
The Yankees' elite pitching staff probably won't provide the Red Sox with many scoring opportunities in their short series, so it's imperative that they come through when given the chance. Lately, Boston hasn't had anyone in its lineup to feel confident about when they step to the plate with runners on.
Role players regressing
As great as guys like Willson Contreras, Caleb Durbin, and Wilyer Abreu were throughout the Red Sox' incredible midseason turnaround, it was the role players who powered their surge. Mickey Gasper, Jahmai Jones, Nick Sogard, Anthony Seigler, and Andruw Monasterio were instrumental in resurrecting Boston's season.
Gasper has cooled off, though no one expected him to sustain his Barry Bonds-like run. Jahmai Jones is 4 for his last 22 (.182) with nine strikeouts, suddenly making him a playoff roster cut candidate. Sogard is still hitting, but his .758 OPS so far in September suggests regression to the mean. Seigler is hurt. Monasterio posted a .578 OPS in August and is 0-for-11 so far in September, putting him on the playoff roster bubble.
That group deserves immense credit for getting the Red Sox here, but it cannot be counted on to propel the club through the postseason.
Erik Miller experiencing command issues
Boston's bullpen is arguably its biggest strength heading into the postseason. The back end with Garrett Whitlock, Tyron Guerrero, and Aroldis Chapman is elite.
We would've included trade deadline addition Erik Miller in that group last month, when he allowed only one earned run with 20 strikeouts and just three walks across his first 11 appearances with the Red Sox. His performance so far this month, however, has been alarming.
Miller, acquired from the San Francisco Giants in the Marcelo Mayer trade, has allowed four earned runs with six walks and six strikeouts through five appearances (4.1 IP) in September. His command struggles were a question mark upon his joining the club, and it appears that issue has reemerged with less than two weeks until the playoffs.
After Wednesday's poor outing against the Texas Rangers (2 H, 3 ER, 1 BB), Miller attributed his recent struggles to his mechanics. The Red Sox will hope that whatever the problem is, it's a quick fix, because Miller will be counted on to be their most reliable left-handed reliever not named Aroldis Chapman.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox recalled Anthony Seigler less than a week ago to help fill the roster gap left by Eli White's foot injury. The switch-hitting infielder had contributed during a stretch that lifted Boston into playoff contention.
That fill-in role has already been cut short. Seigler went on the injured list September 13 with a right wrist issue, and the latest update paints a discouraging picture for his availability going forward.
The Red Sox are 82-70 with 10 games left in the regular season. The playoff spot is within reach. The roster is getting thinner.
Infielder Shut Down From Baseball Activities
Seigler has been shut down from all baseball activities for at least a week, according to MassLive's Chris Cotillo.
The wrist flared up again during a plate appearance on Sunday, and he now appears doubtful to return during the regular season.
The timeline makes the math difficult. A minimum of seven days without baseball activities leaves almost no runway to ramp back up before the final game of the season. Even an optimistic recovery would push his return deep into October, if it comes at all.
What Seigler Brought to Boston
Seigler arrived from the Milwaukee Brewers in February alongside Caleb Durbin and Andruw Monasterio. After joining the big league roster in late June, he became part of a stretch that saw Boston win at a historic pace.
He delivered a 4-for-5 performance against the Blue Jays in July that included a leadoff homer and two doubles. In August, he lined a ninth-inning triple that gave Boston the lead against the Marlins when the team needed it most.
Across 171 plate appearances this season, Seigler slashed .250/.331/.405 with three home runs and 13 RBIs. His positional versatility and switch-hitting made him a valuable bench piece for a team building toward October.
Final Word for the Red Sox
Anthony Seigler was brought back to help. Less than a week later, the Red Sox are dealing with another absence.
The wrist issue is the latest in a string of roster hits Boston has absorbed down the stretch. White is done for the regular season. Ceddanne Rafaela remains out until next week. The depth that carried this team through the summer is being tested heading into the final 10 games.
Seigler did enough during his time on the field to earn the recall. Whether he gets another chance this year depends on how far the Red Sox go in October.

item.title: [roundtable.io] Could Spring Training Standout Replace Injured Eli White on Boston Red Sox Playoff Roster?
item.dc:creator: Zach Coe

item.content:encoded:
Alex Cora said Braiden Ward would be a factor in October.
The Boston Red Sox outfield depth took a major hit ahead of last Friday’s series opener against the Kansas City Royals as the team placed Eli White on the 10-day injured list with a right foot ligament injury, with no timetable for his return. The 32-year-old outfielder not only filled in admirably for the injured Ceddanne Rafaela, but was also slated to play an important role on the postseason roster as the fourth outfielder and pinch runner off the bench. With White now unlikely to return before the postseason, could the Red Sox turn to spring-training standout Braiden Ward to fill the role?
About Ward
The Red Sox acquired Ward in an offseason deal with the Colorado Rockies in exchange for left-handed reliever Brennan Bernardino. The 27-year-old outfielder became one of the biggest storylines of Red Sox spring training, seeing ample playing time as many of Boston's outfield options, including Roman Anthony, Wilyer Abreu and Rafaela, represented their countries in the World Baseball Classic. In 27 Grapefruit League games, Ward hit .378/.509/.444/.953 while stealing 19 bases, setting a single-season spring training record. Ward's dynamic speed caught the eye of now-former manager Alex Cora, who told reporters on several occasions that the 27-year-old would be a factor come October.
After missing the team's opening-day roster amid an already crowded outfield, Ward spent the entire 2026 season in Triple-A Worcester. In 107 games with the WooSox, Ward hit just .238/.356/.355/.711 but set a record for most stolen bases in a single season for a Red Sox Triple-A club with 58 and counting.
There's just one problem...
While Ward seems like a slam-dunk option to fill White's role on the postseason roster, it is not as simple as just recalling him from Triple-A, as he's not on the 40-man roster. The Red Sox 40-man roster currently sits at 39; however, the impending returns of Garrett Crochet, Tanner Houck and Johan Oviedo mean the team will have to either designate two players for assignment or move someone to the 60-day IL.
Luckily, there are several candidates for the latter: in White, should he be unable to return for the postseason, designated hitter Masataka Yoshida, utility man Anthony Seigler and reliever Justin Slaten, all of whom appear unlikely to return prior to the end of the season.
Is Ward actually an option?
Interim manager Chad Tracy was asked about the possibility of Ward joining the big-league club during his weekly appearance on WEEI's 'Rich and Ken with Ted Johnson' Show on Wednesday afternoon. "I think that'd be considered for sure," he said when asked about the possibility of Ward joining the big-league team. "It's really hard to predict what a roster could look like, but you definitely can't ignore a 60-stolen-base player," he continued.
However, Tracy cautioned that a pinch runner is a last resort for a team when it's trailing, and teams must consider other options, like whether it would be more valuable to add another right-handed bat or a better defender to the roster. Though Ward does profile as an above-average outfield defender.
Up next for the Sox
After falling 4-2 in Tuesday night's series opener, the Red Sox will look to even up the three-game set with the Texas Rangers in game two of three from Globe Life Field on Wednesday night. Rookie left-hander Jake Bennett (9-7, 3.69 ERA) will get the start for Boston opposite fellow southpaw MacKenzie Gore (8-11, 4.62 ERA) for Texas. First pitch is set for 8:05 p.m. ET.

item.title: [The Boston Globe] The Red Sox took great pains to build depth in the offseason, and the results are paying off - The Boston Globe

item.content:encoded:
ARLINGTON, Texas — For the Red Sox, the vision of contention in 2026 seemed straightforward.
The team’s championship window had been pried open by the presence of a pair of cornerstones, with Garrett Crochet anchoring the rotation and Roman Anthony representing a lineup anchor not only for this year but several seasons to come.
But while the Sox are amid a magic-number countdown to a playoff berth, they’ve done so without Anthony and Crochet for most of the year. Their season has been saved in no small part by players who have emerged from obscurity to play critical roles — with essential contributions coming from Andruw Monasterio, Anthony Seigler, Mickey Gasper, Tsung-Che Cheng, Jahmai Jones, Tyron Guerrero, and more.
“I don’t think anybody had that on the drawing board,” said interim manager Chad Tracy with a chuckle. “They were asked to play a lot, and they produced. And if they didn’t, we were in trouble. It’s a huge piece of the 2026 season, no question.”
Of course, while no one expected the outsized impact of players who began the year as big league backups or in Triple-A, the Sox also took considerable pains to build organizational depth through a variety of transactions.
Whether it was an expanded version of the trade that brought Caleb Durbin from Milwaukee to include Monasterio and Seigler, or waiver claims of Cheng and Gasper, or a minor league deal for Guerrero, the season has been a case study in the notion that perceived little moves can have a huge impact.
“Every move and every decision matters,” said assistant general manager Mike Groopman, who oversees the team’s acquisitions group. “The big ones, whether it’s a larger free agent deal, [or] a larger, more high-profile trade, is naturally going to get a lot of attention.
“I don’t think this is unique to the Red Sox. There are 29 other teams that try to and do a very good job about caring about the ‘little’ things. But I think what we really try to reinforce is … that year over year, around the game, you see things that seem ‘little’ that end up being really impactful and big. [Deals that] seemed like small moves at the outset end up having a much, much larger impact commensurate with what would have been perceived at the time as a ‘larger’ move.”
Players who evolve from theoretical depth to become big league contributors excite numerous corners of an organization. The primary credit for those contributions, of course, belongs with a player, but they still often represent the combined efforts of personnel in scouting who identify the player’s potential contributions, player development personnel who help the player build on preexisting strengths and abilities in the minors, and big league staffers who help the players to perform at the game’s highest level.
Take Guerrero. After brief stints in the big leagues in 2018 and 2019, he’d become a journeyman, shuffling between organizations — and countries — but unable to forge a way back to the big leagues despite elite velocity.
But the Sox — who’d been interested in signing Guerrero before he pitched in the NPB in Japan in 2025 — remained intrigued, thanks in part to strong scouting recommendations from Kento Matsumoto in Japan and Manny Nanita in the Dominican Winter League. After they signed Guerrero to a minor league deal in the offseason, player development officials worked with him on some minor grip changes that unlocked significantly improved command with a sinker that regularly reached triple digits.
Guerrero’s dominance this year in Triple-A (0.92 ERA) essentially forced the Sox to call him up, and the 35-year-old emerged as a late-innings force from late June to late August (before shoulder fatigue led to a bad outing followed by a trip to the injured list), posting a 2.13 ERA over a 23-appearance stretch.
Again, the lion’s share of the credit goes to Guerrero for the work he did to fight his way back to the big leagues. But his emergence embodies the sort of under-the-radar acquisition that helped save the Sox’ season.
“The connection and integration between acquisition and development is really important,” said Groopman. “Guerrero and our [player development] group put a lot of time into [those changes] in the spring and the early season, to get him to a point where he was able to lock in some of these changes and unlock what was super obvious arm talent into something that was translating more consistently onto the major league mound.”
Of course, talent alone doesn’t dictate success once a depth player gets to the big leagues. They must also have the opportunity to contribute — and, in many cases, the freedom to fail while getting their bearings.
Tracy, who spent time with nearly all of this year’s depth contributors in Triple-A at the beginning of the year, has been mindful of creating an environment in which call-ups can contribute.
“I’m in the same boat [as them]. I want the freedom to go manage the game [as a first-time big league manager],” said Tracy. “I need to manage a game and feel like if I do something that doesn’t go right, it’s not the end of the world. If I feel that way, then I want the player to feel like, ‘Hey, if you go out there and play second base today and you make an error, move on to the next play.’
“If the culture becomes, ‘If I make a mistake, then all of a sudden I clam up and I get really tight,’ we’re going to have a problem. So you look at them and say, ‘You’re here for a reason: To go play your game. Don’t worry about making a mistake. Move on to the next pitch, next play.’ And they did that, and they were awesome.”
Alex Speier can be reached at alex.speier@globe.com. Follow him @alexspeier.

item.content:encoded:
We've reached the "wake me up for the playoffs" portion of the Boston Red Sox season.
The Red Sox have 12 games remaining on their 2026 regular-season schedule. As of Monday, they sit comfortably in the second American League Wild Card spot with a six-game lead. They're 4.5 games behind the New York Yankees in the Wild Card standings, so barring a shocking development, they'll visit the New York Yankees in the Wild Card Series for the second consecutive year.
Which 26 players will the Red Sox bring with them to the Bronx? Who's on the chopping block? Here's our 26-man playoff roster projection with 15 days until Game 1:
MORE RED SOX
Catcher (2): Adley Rutschman, Connor Wong
Cuts: None
The Red Sox could theoretically cut Wong since he'd barely see the field with Rutschman healthy. If Rutschman went down in that scenario, Mickey Gasper could go behind the plate... but that wouldn't be pretty.
Here's the problem with that approach: If Rutschman gets hurt and the Red Sox add a replacement catcher mid-series, Rutschman would be ineligible for the next playoff round. So if he got hurt in the Wild Card Series, he'd be ineligible for the ALDS and eligible to return in the ALCS.
Putting Wong on the playoff roster ensures that if Rutschman goes down, they won't need to add a mid-series replacement with Wong and Gasper already on board. And while Wong isn't exactly Pudge Rodriguez defensively, he's better than Gasper behind the dish.
Infield (7): Willson Contreras, Trevor Story, Caleb Durbin, Isiah Kiner-Falefa, Nick Sogard, Mickey Gasper, Andruw Monasterio
Cuts: Curtis Mead (IL), Anthony Seigler (IL)
Even with Wong on the roster, Gasper's incredible offensive upside shown in August earns him a roster spot as a bench bat. Monasterio is on the bubble, but recent injuries may have cleared his path to a bench role.
It doesn't look like Mead (wrist) will be healthy in time for the start of the postseason.
Outfield (5): Jarren Duran, Wilyer Abreu, Ceddanne Rafaela, Roman Anthony, Jahmai Jones
Cuts: Eli White (IL), Masataka Yoshida (IL), Nate Eaton
The big question mark here is White's health, as the speedster was recently placed on the 10-day injured list with a foot ligament injury. He'll play a key bench role if healthy, but if he isn't, Jones or Eaton are the top candidates for that fifth outfield spot. We're leaning Jones because of his ability to mash left-handers.
Yoshida (hamstring) probably isn't coming back this year.
Starting rotation (3): Sonny Gray, Payton Tolle, Ranger Suarez
Cuts: Patrick Sandoval
Sandoval just hasn't been reliable, so he draws the short straw. Jake Bennett and the returning Garrett Crochet move to the bullpen -- assuming Crochet is healthy enough to give one or two quality innings in relief.
Bullpen (9): Garrett Crochet, Jake Bennett, Brayan Bello, Greg Weissert, Wyatt Olds, Erik Miller, Tyron Guerrero, Garrett Whitlock, Aroldis Chapman
Cuts: Justin Slaten (IL), Tanner Houck (IL), Johan Oviedo (IL), Alec Gamboa, Jovani Moran, Raymond Burgos
If Slaten's elbow is healthy, he's in, but it doesn't currently look like it will be since he was recently shut down from throwing.
Crochet is trending toward being ready just in time for October. So is Houck, but he hasn't pitched in a big-league game since May 2025, and he hasn't looked sharp in his rehab outings. While his upside is intriguing, we'd leave him off the initial playoff roster.
Brayan Bello makes the cut as a bulk arm after excelling in that role throughout the second half.

item.content:encoded:
Willson Contreras is back with the Red Sox, activated Sunday from the injured list for their finale against the Royals. He collected two hits and a walk in the 4-1 win.
The Red Sox didn’t need to think hard about how to open a spot on the active roster: infielder Anthony Seigler went on the injured list with a right wrist issue.
“We talked a lot about as guys were getting healthy, the conversation was like, ‘What are you going to do?’” interim manager Chad Tracy said. “Stuff’s going to happen, which it always does.”
Contreras missed a dozen games because of a left hamstring strain.
After playing through the leg problem for about a month, Contreras asked the front office to let him more thoroughly rest, figuring a September timeout would serve him well down the stretch and into the playoffs.
On his first day back, he tested it plenty — hustling to first base and advancing to second on an error, moving from first to third on a single.
“I ran a lot today on the field, and my hammy feels pretty good,” Contreras said. “I won’t lie: If I wasn’t feeling really good in [Double-A] Portland, I wasn’t going to play tonight.”
Tracy said: “The point of [going on the IL] was to get [the hamstring] to a point where he felt confident in it, where he can go out and play and not have to worry. And at least like to think we’ve got to that point, which is good.”
In a two-game tuneup with Double-A Portland, Contreras went 2 for 7 with three strikeouts and no walks.
His appearance Saturday yielded a strange episode in the fourth inning. After a ball moved the count to 1-and-1, he called timeout, seemingly to get pine tar. Plate umpire Daniel Bytheway called him back to the plate.
Contreras then all but stopped participating in the plate appearance, leaving the bat on his shoulders for the next four pitches. He struck out looking.
On his way back to the dugout, drawing boos from the Portland crowd, Contreras tossed his bat back toward the plate.
“I didn’t even know until somebody showed it to me this [Sunday] morning,” Tracy said before the game. “I haven’t even seen him and asked him that yet. I think that’s something to do with pine tar.”
Contreras said later Sunday: “I don’t know. You can go ask the umpire. His name is Gary. Thank you.”
The Red Sox didn’t have a diagnosis on Seigler, who hurt himself on a seemingly random swing Saturday, but intended to send him for tests in the coming days.
As the rotation turns
The Red Sox will keep their starting pitchers in line against the Rangers: Patrick Sandoval on Tuesday, Jake Bennett on Wednesday, Sonny Gray on Thursday. Brayan Bello is bumped back to the bullpen following a one-start cameo.
Rehab roundup
The Red Sox will bring Tyron Guerrero (right shoulder inflammation) to Texas and activate him during the Rangers series. They haven’t decided which day. He is eligible to return Wednesday.
Ceddanne Rafaela (right quad strain) told NESN he is planning to return for the Rays series next weekend.
“We’ll call that a goal. It’s not a guarantee,” Tracy said. “It really is dependent on strength numbers in the quad and making sure that’s appropriate, and then he gets through all the sprint volume stuff first, and then we’ll see where he’s at.”
The Sox will leave it up to Rafaela, Tracy added, whether he wants to go on a rehab assignment before returning. Triple-A Worcester is the last affiliate still in season.
Justin Slaten (right elbow inflammation) still has not resumed throwing.
Guest of honor
Beverly native Beckett Connolly, a 10-year-old liver cancer survivor and transplant recipient, threw out a ceremonial first pitch — to hefty applause from the Fenway Park crowd.
